pos: n. (the Assyrian king who first carried Israel into captivity)
etymology: Akkadian Tukulti-apil-Esharra, "my trust is in the son of Esharra," the god Ninurta; rendered in the KJV as Tiglathpileser and, once, Tilgathpilneser.
biblical_def: Tiglath-pileser III is the Assyrian king under whom the LORD’s judgment on the northern kingdom began in earnest. In the days of Pekah, he “took Ijon, and Abelbethmaachah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor, and Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them captive to Assyria” (2 Kings 15:29), the opening act of the deportation that would end the ten tribes’ independent existence within a generation. His deeper entanglement with Judah is a case study in the folly of unbelief: when Syria and Israel combined against wicked King Ahaz, Ahaz refused the LORD’s own offer of a sign through Isaiah (Isaiah 7:10–12) and instead “sent messengers to Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, saying, I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me” (2 Kings 16:7), stripping the temple treasury to pay the price. Assyria came — and stayed, a permanent and eventually fatal presence in Judah’s affairs. Ahaz then traveled to Damascus to meet his new overlord and there saw a pagan altar he was so taken with that he had its pattern copied for the LORD’s own house (2 Kings 16:10). The Chronicler names the same king by his fuller Assyrian title, Tilgathpilneser, and states plainly that it was the LORD Himself, not mere geopolitics, who “stirred up the spirit” of this pagan king to carry the Transjordan tribes away (1 Chronicles 5:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Tiglath-pileser; he is the Assyrian king who first deported the northern tribes and whom King Ahaz hired against Syria and Israel, at the cost of the temple treasury and Judah's independence.
webster_full: TIGLATH-PILESER, n. A king of Assyria who deported the northern tribes of Israel and was later hired by King Ahaz of Judah.
ASSYRIA, n. An ancient and powerful empire of the Mesopotamian region, the instrument of the LORD's judgment on the northern kingdom.
CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner or held in bondage; in Scripture, especially the exile of Israel and Judah for covenant unfaithfulness.
TRIBUTE, n. A stated sum or other valuable thing paid by one ruler or nation to another, in acknowledgment of submission.
APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of one's professed principles or faith; Ahaz's turning to pagan Assyria and a pagan altar pattern is a case study.
scriptures: 2 Kings 15:29

In the days of Pekah king of Israel came Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, and took Ijon, and Abelbethmaachah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor, and Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them captive to Assyria.
2 Kings 16:7

So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, saying, I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria, and out of the hand of the king of Israel, which rise up against me.
2 Kings 16:10

And king Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, and saw an altar that was at Damascus: and king Ahaz sent to Urijah the priest the fashion of the altar, and the pattern of it, according to all the workmanship thereof.
1 Chronicles 5:26

And the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgathpilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away, even the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and brought them unto Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan, unto this day.
corruption_summary: A pagan Assyrian king whose deportation records match, in name and campaign, the Assyrians' own royal inscriptions is inconvenient for any theory that the historical books are late, unreliable legend.
corruption_paragraphs: Minimalist Old Testament criticism, quick to treat the kings' narratives as tendentious later composition, is quietest exactly where the evidence is strongest: extra-biblical Assyrian annals independently name Tiglath-pileser III's western campaigns, his reception of tribute from a king named Jehoahaz of Judah (Ahaz's fuller throne name), and his deportations from the very regions 2 Kings 15:29 lists. The convergence of an ancient pagan empire's own boasting inscriptions with Israel's inspired history is not the pattern a late, careless legend produces.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah's own commentary on this exact king: Ahaz, offered a sign as deep as hell or as high as heaven and refusing to ask (Isaiah 7:11–12), hired the very empire that would become “the rod of mine anger” (Isaiah 10:5) against his own house. Unbelief that will not trust the LORD's word inevitably trusts something else, and the something else always proves a harder master than the trouble it was hired to solve.
roots_summary: Akkadian Tukulti-apil-Esharra, my trust is in the son of Esharra; Hebrew golah (H1473), captivity, exile; ebed (H5650), servant; ma'al (H4604), trespass, unfaithfulness.
roots_lines: Akkadian Tukulti-apil-Esharra — my trust is in the son of Esharra, the god Ninurta.
Hebrew golah (H1473) — captivity, the exiled company; the fate Tiglath-pileser began for Israel.
Hebrew ebed (H5650) — servant; Ahaz's own self-description to the Assyrian king.
Hebrew ma'al (H4604) — trespass, unfaithfulness; the Chronicler's verdict on the deported tribes (1 Chronicles 5:25).
Hebrew ur (H5782) — to stir up, arouse; the verb of the LORD stirring the king's own spirit.
usage: “Carried them captive to Assyria” — the beginning of the northern exile.
“I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me” — Ahaz's fatal appeal.
“The God of Israel stirred up the spirit of... Tilgathpilneser” — the LORD's sovereignty over a pagan king.

pos: n. (the Egyptian king who slew Josiah at Megiddo)
etymology: Egyptian throne name, rendered in the KJV as Pharaohnechoh (2 Kings) and Pharaohnecho (Jeremiah); Necho II of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty.
biblical_def: Pharaoh-necho is the king of Egypt whose march north against the crumbling Assyrian empire ended the reign, and the life, of good King Josiah. Marching to relieve his Assyrian allies at Carchemish, Necho found his path blocked: “Josiah had prepared the temple, Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates: and Josiah went out against him” (2 Chronicles 35:20). Necho sent word that his quarrel was not with Judah, but Josiah, for reasons Scripture does not fully explain, went out anyway — “he slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him” (2 Kings 23:29), plunging Judah into the mourning still remembered in Zechariah’s day (Zechariah 12:11). Necho then treated Judah as a client state without ceremony, deposing Josiah’s son and installing another in his place: “Pharaohnechoh made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the room of Josiah his father, and turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away: and he came to Egypt, and died there” (2 Kings 23:34). Necho’s own moment of imperial confidence did not last; the LORD sent Nebuchadnezzar to crush him decisively at the very city he had marched to save — “the army of Pharaohnecho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote” (Jeremiah 46:2), the battle that shifted the balance of the ancient world from Egypt to Babylon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Pharaoh-necho; he is the Egyptian king who slew Josiah at Megiddo, deposed his son, and was himself later crushed by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish.
webster_full: PHARAOH-NECHO, n. A king of Egypt who killed King Josiah in battle at Megiddo and was later defeated by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish.
MEGIDDO, n. A fortified city of northern Israel, site of several decisive battles, including the death of King Josiah.
JOSIAH, n. A righteous king of Judah, noted for his reforms and the rediscovery of the Book of the Law, slain by Pharaoh-necho.
CARCHEMISH, n. An ancient city on the Euphrates, site of Nebuchadnezzar's decisive victory over Egypt.
TRIBUTARY, a. Paying tribute to another as an acknowledgment of submission or subjection; Judah's state under Egypt after Josiah's death.
scriptures: 2 Kings 23:29
In his days Pharaohnechoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates: and king Josiah went against him; and he slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him.
2 Chronicles 35:20
After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates: and Josiah went out against him.
2 Kings 23:34
And Pharaohnechoh made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the room of Josiah his father, and turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away: and he came to Egypt, and died there.
Jeremiah 46:2

Against Egypt, against the army of Pharaohnecho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah.
corruption_summary: The precise, unflattering-to-everyone account of Josiah's needless death and Egypt's later crushing at Carchemish is exactly the sober, unglamorous record a court-flattering later invention would not produce for either nation.
corruption_paragraphs: Skeptical historiography that treats the historical books as national self-flattery struggles with this episode from every angle: Judah's own best king dies pointlessly against a foreign power that explicitly disclaimed any quarrel with him, and Judah's conqueror-of-convenience is himself humiliated a few years later. A text manufactured to glorify Israel's kings does not record its most righteous king dying in an apparently avoidable battle he was warned against.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sober reminder that even a godly king's record ends imperfectly this side of glory; Josiah's reforms were genuine and the LORD's own verdict on his reign stands (2 Kings 23:25), yet his final act was not one of simple faith, and Scripture records the consequence without flattering it — a pattern of unsparing honesty about even its heroes that marks the record as true history, not hagiography.
roots_summary: Egyptian throne name Necho (Nekau); Hebrew Mĕgiddown (H4023), Megiddo; nakah (H5221), to smite; karath (H3772), to cut off.
roots_lines: Egyptian throne-name Nekau — rendered Pharaohnechoh/Pharaohnecho in the KJV.
Hebrew Megiddown (H4023) — Megiddo, the fortified valley where Josiah fell.
Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to smite; the verb of Josiah's death and of Nebuchadnezzar's later victory.
Hebrew perath (H6578) — the Euphrates; the river both battles were fought beside.
Hebrew malak (H4427) — to reign, be king; the office Necho conferred and withdrew at will over Judah.
usage: “He slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him” — Josiah's death.
“Turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away” — Egypt's brief control of Judah's throne.
“Which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote” — Necho's own later defeat at Carchemish.

pos: n. (the ancient city of Melchizedek, identified with Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Shalem (H8004), peace, from shalom, peace, wholeness, completeness.
biblical_def: Salem is the city of the mysterious priest-king who meets Abraham returning victorious from the rescue of Lot: “Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God” (Genesis 14:18). The name means peace, and the psalmist later fixes Salem’s location beyond doubt by pairing it with Israel’s own holy hill: “In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Zion” (Psalm 76:2) — Salem is Jerusalem under its most ancient recorded name, centuries before David captured it from the Jebusites. The author of Hebrews, expounding Melchizedek’s significance as a type of Christ, draws directly on the name’s meaning: this priest-king met Abraham, blessed him, received tithes from him, and was “first being by interpretation King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of peace” (Hebrews 7:2). The order is deliberate and doctrinally loaded — righteousness first, then peace, exactly the gospel order in which Christ, the greater Melchizedek, brings peace only on the ground of accomplished righteousness (Romans 5:1). Salem’s brief appearance in Genesis thus becomes, in the hands of the New Testament, a name freighted with the whole logic of the gospel centuries before Sinai.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no separate entry for Salem under this exact heading beyond noting it as Jerusalem's ancient name; the word means peace, and the city is first named as Melchizedek's seat in Genesis 14.
webster_full: SALEM, n. The ancient name of Jerusalem, meaning peace, first mentioned as the city of Melchizedek.
MELCHIZEDEK, n. The priest-king of Salem who blessed Abraham; a type of Christ's eternal priesthood.
TITHE, n. The tenth part of one's income or produce, set apart as an offering; Abraham's gift to Melchizedek.
TYPE, n. In theology, a person, event, or thing in the Old Testament that prefigures a corresponding reality in the New.
RIGHTEOUSNESS, n. Purity of heart and rectitude of life; conformity to the divine law; in the gospel, imputed through Christ.
scriptures: Genesis 14:18
And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.
Psalm 76:2
In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Zion.
Hebrews 7:1
For this Melchisedec, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him;
Hebrews 7:2
To whom also Abraham gave a tenth part of all; first being by interpretation King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of peace;
corruption_summary: A New Testament writer building an elaborate typological argument on the precise meaning of an obscure Old Testament place-name is not the move of a text inventing doctrine loosely from vague sources.
corruption_paragraphs: Historical-critical readings that treat the Melchizedek episode as a late, awkwardly inserted fragment with no real theological weight in its original Genesis context cannot easily explain the New Testament's own confidence in building a load-bearing argument for Christ's priesthood on it (Hebrews 5–7) — a fragile textual accident does not bear that kind of apostolic weight; a genuine, providentially placed anticipation of Christ does.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gospel order Hebrews draws from the name itself: righteousness before peace, never peace apart from righteousness. Every modern impulse to seek peace — personal, social, ecclesiastical — while setting aside the prior demand of righteousness inverts the very order this ancient name was chosen by the Spirit to teach.
roots_summary: Hebrew Shalem (H8004), peace; shalom (H7965), peace, wholeness; tsedeq (H6664), righteousness; ma'aser (H4643), tithe, tenth part.
roots_lines: Hebrew Shalem (H8004) — peace; the name of the ancient city itself.
Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, wholeness, completeness; the root word behind Salem.
Hebrew tsedeq (H6664) — righteousness; the first half of Melchizedek's own name and title-order.
Hebrew ma'aser (H4643) — tithe, tenth part; what Abraham gave the king of Salem.
Hebrew kohen (H3548) — priest; Melchizedek's office as king of this city.
usage: “Melchizedek king of Salem” — the city's first appearance in Scripture.
“In Salem also is his tabernacle” — the psalmist's identification with Zion.
“King of Salem, which is, King of peace” — the New Testament's typological reading of the name.

pos: n. (the second son of Ham, ancestor and Hebrew name of the Egyptian nation)
etymology: Hebrew Mitsrayim (H4714), a dual form, likely reflecting Upper and Lower Egypt; the ordinary Hebrew word for Egypt itself throughout the Old Testament.
biblical_def: Mizraim is named second among the sons of Ham in the Table of Nations: “the sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim, Put, and Canaan” (Genesis 10:6), and his own descendants are listed at length — “Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim” (Genesis 10:13), the opening line of a roster the Chronicler repeats without change centuries later (1 Chronicles 1:8, 11). What makes Mizraim distinctive among the Table of Nations entries is that his personal name became, throughout the rest of the Old Testament, the ordinary Hebrew word for the nation and land of Egypt itself — every reference to Israel coming up “out of Mizraim” (the literal Hebrew behind “out of Egypt” in Exodus 20:2 and hundreds of other verses) is, strictly, an appeal to this ancestor’s name. Egypt’s dual character as both a place of temporary refuge (for Abraham in famine, Genesis 12; for Jacob’s house, Genesis 46; for the infant Christ, Matthew 2:13–15) and the paradigmatic house of bondage (Exodus 20:2) is thus bound up, at the level of the Hebrew language itself, with the name of one of Noah’s great-grandsons.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Mizraim; he is the second son of Ham in the Table of Nations, and his name became the standing Hebrew word for Egypt throughout the Old Testament.
webster_full: MIZRAIM, n. The second son of Ham, ancestor of the Egyptians; his name is the ordinary Hebrew word for Egypt.
EGYPT, n. An ancient and powerful nation of northeastern Africa, called Mizraim in the Hebrew Scriptures.
HAM, n. The second son of Noah, whose descendants settled Africa and parts of Canaan and Arabia.
TABLE OF NATIONS, n. The genealogy in Genesis 10 tracing the nations of the earth from Noah's three sons.
BONDAGE, n. Slavery; a state of subjection; Israel's condition in Egypt before the Exodus.
scriptures: Genesis 10:6
And the sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan.
Genesis 10:13
And Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim,
1 Chronicles 1:8
The sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.
1 Chronicles 1:11
And Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim,
corruption_summary: A genealogical table whose entries correspond in outline to genuinely attested ancient peoples of Africa and Arabia is a poor fit for a document dismissed as late mythological invention.
corruption_paragraphs: Higher-critical readings that treat Genesis 10 as a late, schematic literary construction with no real ethnographic memory behind it have to explain its broad correspondence with genuinely attested ancient peoples and regions — the association of Mizraim's line with African and Egyptian-adjacent territories is not the kind of accuracy a purely theological literary fiction, invented centuries after the fact with no access to real historical memory, tends to produce.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD's providence governs the table of nations itself, “that they should seek the Lord... and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Acts 17:26–27). Mizraim's descendants became a nation that was, in turn, both refuge and furnace for the covenant people — even the pagan nations of Genesis 10 stand inside, not outside, the LORD's sovereign ordering of history toward Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew Mitsrayim (H4714), Egypt, a dual form; Cham (H2526), Ham; goy (H1471), nation; bayith avadim, house of bondage.
roots_lines: Hebrew Mitsrayim (H4714) — a dual form, likely reflecting Upper and Lower Egypt.
Hebrew Cham (H2526) — Ham, Mizraim's father, whose name means hot or warm.
Hebrew goy (H1471) — nation; the category the Table of Nations organizes Noah's descendants into.
Hebrew ebed (H5650) — servant, slave; the root behind bondage, Egypt's later paradigmatic role.
Hebrew yatsa' (H3318) — to go out, come forth; the verb of the Exodus “out of Mizraim.”
usage: “The sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim” — his place in the Table of Nations.
“Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim” — his own descendants.
“Out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2) — the phrase his name underlies throughout the Old Testament.

pos: n. (a son of Dan, and, separately, a wife of Shaharaim of Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Chushim (H2366), plural form, possibly meaning "those who hasten" or "swiftness," from chush, to make haste.
biblical_def: Hushim is named, in Genesis’s brief account of the household that went down to Egypt with Jacob, as the whole of Dan’s recorded offspring: “And the sons of Dan; Hushim” (Genesis 46:23) — a singular name given in a plural grammatical form, most naturally read as the name of Dan’s one son who founded the entire tribe. The Chronicler preserves a variant of the same name among the descendants of Benjamin, “Shuppim also, and Huppim, the children of Ir, and Hushim, the sons of Aher” (1 Chronicles 7:12), showing the name recurring, as many Hebrew names do, across different tribal lines. A wholly separate Hushim appears two chapters later as a wife: “Shaharaim begat children in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away; Hushim and Baara were his wives” (1 Chronicles 8:8), and her own son’s line is then traced — “of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal” (1 Chronicles 8:11), the ancestor, several generations further on, of the family that produced King Saul (1 Chronicles 8:33). One name, evidently in use among both Dan’s tribe and later Benjamite households, thus threads through two of the twelve tribes’ genealogies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Hushim; the name belongs both to the son who represents the whole tribe of Dan in Genesis 46 and, separately, to a wife of Shaharaim in the genealogy of Benjamin.
webster_full: HUSHIM, n. A name borne by a son of Dan and, separately, by a wife of Shaharaim of the tribe of Benjamin.
TRIBE, n. A family, race, or series of generations descended from the same progenitor; one of the twelve divisions of Israel.
GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of persons or families from an ancestor.
PROGENITOR, n. An ancestor in the direct line; a forefather.
HOUSEHOLD, n. Those who dwell under one roof and compose a family; in Scripture, especially the covenant family unit.
scriptures: Genesis 46:23
And the sons of Dan; Hushim.
1 Chronicles 7:12
Shuppim also, and Huppim, the children of Ir, and Hushim, the sons of Aher.
1 Chronicles 8:8
And Shaharaim begat children in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away; Hushim and Baara were his wives.
1 Chronicles 8:11
And of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal.
corruption_summary: A single name recurring, without confusion, across distinct tribal genealogies compiled centuries apart is the mark of careful transmission, not loose invention.
corruption_paragraphs: Source-critical approaches that treat the tribal lists of Genesis and Chronicles as independently and carelessly assembled fragments cannot easily account for the disciplined way the text keeps Dan's Hushim and Benjamin's Hushim distinct across two different books without ever conflating them — a genuinely careless compiler merges similar names; a careful transmitter of real family records keeps them straight, which is exactly what happens here.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD's own care for the seventy souls who went down into Egypt (Genesis 46:27), each one named, however briefly, because each one mattered to the covenant purpose that would, four hundred years later, bring a nation back out. No name in the register, however small its later record, is there by accident.
roots_summary: Hebrew Chushim (H2366), from chush (H2363), to make haste; ben (H1121), son; ishshah (H802), wife, woman; mishpachah (H4940), family.
roots_lines: Hebrew Chushim (H2366) — possibly those who hasten, from chush, to make haste.
Hebrew ben (H1121) — son; the word introducing Hushim in Genesis 46:23.
Hebrew ishshah (H802) — wife, woman; the Chronicler's word for the second Hushim.
Hebrew mishpachah (H4940) — family, clan; the structuring unit of both genealogies.
Hebrew yalad (H3205) — to bear, beget; the verb governing both lines of descent.
usage: “The sons of Dan; Hushim” — the tribe's founding representative.
“Hushim and Baara were his wives” — a different Hushim, in Benjamin's line.
“Of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal” — her descendants traced onward.

pos: n. (a raiding people of Arabia, the LORD's instrument in Job's first affliction)
etymology: Hebrew Sheba' (H7614), the people of Sheba, a region of southwest Arabia noted in Scripture for trade, wealth, and, here, raiding.
biblical_def: The Sabeans first appear in Scripture as the agents of Job’s first great loss: “the Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away; yea, they have slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee” (Job 1:15), the opening blow in a single terrible day that stripped Job of oxen, asses, and servants before a second messenger could even finish speaking. That this raid, like the Chaldean raid and the fire from heaven that follow in the same chapter, occurs entirely within the permission granted to Satan in the heavenly council (Job 1:12) is the theological key to the whole book — the Sabeans act as free moral agents committing real sin, and yet nothing touches Job outside the bounds the LORD Himself has set. Isaiah later names the Sabeans among the peoples whose wealth will one day come over to Zion in submission — “the labour of Egypt, and merchandise of Ethiopia and of the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over unto thee” (Isaiah 45:14) — a striking reversal of Job’s experience, raiders becoming, in the messianic vision, willing tributaries. Joel names them as the distant slave-market to which Judah’s own captured children would be sold in judgment (Joel 3:8), and Ezekiel numbers them among the exotic foreign lovers Jerusalem, under the figure of an adulterous wife, invited into her bed (Ezekiel 23:42) — the same people appearing across four books as raiders, as future worshippers, as a byword for exile, and as a figure for spiritual adultery.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Sabeans as the people of Sheba in Arabia; Scripture first names them as the raiders who stripped Job of his oxen and servants under Satan's permitted testing.
webster_full: SABEANS, n. The inhabitants of Sheba, a region of Arabia, noted in Scripture for wealth, trade, and raiding.
SHEBA, n. An ancient kingdom of southwestern Arabia, whose queen visited Solomon and whose people are named the Sabeans.
AFFLICTION, n. The state of being afflicted; pain, distress, calamity; in Job's case, permitted but not caused by God directly.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over His creatures, including the bounded permission of evil.
TRIBUTE, n. A stated sum or valuable thing paid by one ruler or nation to another in acknowledgment of submission.
scriptures: Job 1:15
And the Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away; yea, they have slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee.
Isaiah 45:14

Thus saith the LORD, The labour of Egypt, and merchandise of Ethiopia and of the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over unto thee, and they shall be thine: they shall come after thee; in chains they shall come over, and they shall fall down unto thee, they shall make supplication unto thee, saying, Surely God is in thee; and there is none else, there is no God.
Joel 3:8
And I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hand of the children of Judah, and they shall sell them to the Sabeans, to a people far off: for the LORD hath spoken it.
Ezekiel 23:42

And a voice of a multitude being at ease was with her: and with the men of the common sort were brought Sabeans from the wilderness, which put bracelets upon their hands, and beautiful crowns upon their heads.
corruption_summary: A single Arabian people appearing consistently across Job, Isaiah, Joel, and Ezekiel, each time fitting its known ancient reputation for trade and raiding, argues for shared historical memory rather than late literary invention.
corruption_paragraphs: Skeptical dating of Job to a late, artificial wisdom-composition has to explain why its incidental details — a raiding people from Arabia named Sabeans, camels as the marker of great wealth, the patriarchal structure of Job's household — match the world of the patriarchal age rather than any later Israelite setting a post-exilic author would more naturally draw from. The book's setting rings true to an era before, not after, it could easily have been invented.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the compatibilist doctrine of providence the whole book of Job exists to teach: the Sabeans sinned freely and are morally responsible for it, and yet not a hair of the calamity fell outside the LORD's sovereign hedge (Job 1:10,12) — the same truth Joseph later states of his own brothers' sin (Genesis 50:20) and the same truth that governs the greatest crime in history, the crucifixion (Acts 2:23).
roots_summary: Hebrew Sheba' (H7614), Sheba; shalal (H7998), spoil, plunder; nasah (H5254), to test, try; gader (H1447), a hedge, wall.
roots_lines: Hebrew Sheba' (H7614) — Sheba, the Arabian region and people the Sabeans belong to.
Hebrew shalal (H7998) — spoil, plunder; the substance of the Sabeans' raid on Job.
Hebrew nasah (H5254) — to test, try; the governing purpose behind Job's affliction.
Hebrew gader (H1447) — a hedge, wall; the LORD's protective boundary around Job (Job 1:10).
Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to make whole, repay; the restoration that closes the book of Job.
usage: “The Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away” — the opening loss of Job's testing.
“Merchandise of Ethiopia and of the Sabeans... shall come over unto thee” — Isaiah's vision of future submission.
“They shall sell them to the Sabeans, to a people far off” — Joel's word of judgment.

pos: n. (Greek-speaking, Hellenized Jews, distinguished in Acts from the native Hebrew-speaking believers)
etymology: Greek Hellenistes (G1675), from Hellen, a Greek; rendered Grecians in the KJV to distinguish Greek-speaking Jews from ethnic Greeks (rendered "Greeks").
biblical_def: The Grecians of Acts are not ethnic Greeks but Greek-speaking, diaspora-formed Jews, and their first appearance exposes the earliest recorded internal tension in the New Testament church: “there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration” (Acts 6:1), the very occasion that produced the appointment of the first deacons (Acts 6:2–6). The distinction is cultural and linguistic, not doctrinal — both groups were Jewish believers in Jesus — yet it was real enough to require careful pastoral wisdom to resolve without division. The same word appears when Saul, newly converted, “spake boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and disputed against the Grecians: but they went about to slay him” (Acts 9:29), showing that unbelieving Hellenistic Jews could be as hostile to the gospel as any other quarter. The word turns in a wholly positive direction at Antioch, where believers scattered by persecution “spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus” (Acts 11:20), the first recorded systematic preaching of Christ to a Hellenized, partly Gentile-adjacent audience, and the seed of the church that would send out Paul and Barnabas. Centuries earlier, Joel had already used the same underlying Hebrew concept of the Greeks (“the children of Judah and the children of Jerusalem have ye sold unto the Grecians,” Joel 3:6) as a byword for a distant, foreign slave market — the very people who, by Acts, had become some of the earliest hearers of the gospel that would one day be preached “to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Grecian as a native of Greece, or one skilled in the Greek language; the New Testament word names Hellenized, Greek-speaking Jews, first appearing in the church's earliest internal conflict over neglected widows.
webster_full: GRECIAN, n. A native of Greece; in Scripture, a Greek-speaking, Hellenized Jew of the dispersion, distinguished from native Hebrew-speaking Jews.
HEBREW, n. A descendant of Abraham; in Acts 6, specifically a native Aramaic or Hebrew-speaking Jew, as distinguished from a Grecian.
DEACON, n. A church officer whose office, first instituted in Acts 6, involves the care of the church's temporal and charitable needs.
DISPERSION, n. The scattering of the Jewish people among the Gentile nations; the setting that produced Greek-speaking Jewish communities.
MURMURING, n. Complaint uttered in a low, discontented tone; the sin Israel repeatedly committed in the wilderness, and a danger even within the early church.
scriptures: Acts 6:1
And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration.
Acts 9:29
And he spake boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and disputed against the Grecians: but they went about to slay him.
Acts 11:20
And some of them were men of Cyprus and Cyrene, which, when they were come to Antioch, spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus.
Joel 3:6
The children also of Judah and the children of Jerusalem have ye sold unto the Grecians, that ye might remove them far from their border.
corruption_summary: A narrative that records the earliest church's own internal ethnic-linguistic friction, rather than hiding it, is the mark of honest history, not a triumphalist later legend of the church's founding.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern intersectional readings eager to recast Acts 6 as a template for perpetual identity-based grievance politics within the church miss the text's actual resolution: the apostles did not form a permanent Grecian caucus or institutionalize the grievance, they appointed godly, Spirit-filled men (several bearing Greek names themselves, Acts 6:5) to serve both groups, and the murmuring ceased as the word of God increased (Acts 6:7). The biblical pattern is concrete, servant-hearted remedy under recognized church office, not the perpetuation of grievance as identity.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel does not erase cultural and linguistic distinctions among believers, but it does demand that no such distinction be allowed to produce practical injustice in the care of Christ's own people — the same gospel that produced murmuring Grecians in Acts 6 produced, within the same chapter, deacons appointed to serve them, and by Acts 11, Grecians themselves hearing and receiving the good news of the very Lord their fellow believers had once neglected them under.
roots_summary: Greek Hellenistes (G1675), a Hellenist, Greek-speaking Jew, from Hellen (G1672), a Greek; gogguzo (G1111), to murmur; diakonia (G1248), ministry, service.
roots_lines: Greek Hellenistes (G1675) — a Hellenist; a Greek-speaking, culturally Hellenized Jew.
Greek Hellen (G1672) — a Greek; the root behind Hellenistes and behind the English Grecian.
Greek gogguzo (G1111) — to murmur; the sin named at the root of Acts 6:1, echoing Israel's wilderness murmuring.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — ministry, service; the daily distribution the Grecian widows were being denied.
Greek euangelizo (G2097) — to preach good news; the verb of Acts 11:20's turning point.
usage: “A murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews” — the church's earliest recorded internal conflict.
“He... disputed against the Grecians: but they went about to slay him” — Saul's early, dangerous ministry.
“Spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus” — the gospel's advance at Antioch.

pos: n. (the Levitical clan descended from Hebron, son of Kohath)
etymology: Hebrew Chevroni (H2276), from Chevron, a son of Kohath; not to be confused with the city of the same name in Judah.
biblical_def: The Hebronites are one of the four Levitical clans descended from Kohath, named for their ancestor Hebron son of Kohath — a man wholly distinct from the city of the same name in Judah. The census of the Kohathites lists them plainly: “of Kohath was the family of the Amramites, and the family of the Izeharites, and the family of the Hebronites, and the family of the Uzzielites: these are the families of the Kohathites” (Numbers 3:27), a listing repeated in the wilderness census a generation later (Numbers 26:58). By David’s day the clan had grown into a substantial force in the kingdom’s administration: “of the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his brethren, men of valour, a thousand and seven hundred, were officers among them of Israel on this side Jordan westward in all the business of the LORD, and in the service of the king” (1 Chronicles 26:30), with a further company under Jerijah stationed east of Jordan (1 Chronicles 26:31–32) — Levites serving not only at the altar but in civil administration under a king who understood that even the kingdom’s business belonged, in the end, to the LORD. The clan’s own genealogy within Hebron’s house is further detailed: “of the sons of Hebron; Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth” (1 Chronicles 23:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Hebronites; they are one of the four Levitical clans of Kohath, named for their ancestor Hebron, and served both at the altar and in David's civil administration.
webster_full: HEBRONITES, n. A Levitical family descended from Hebron, son of Kohath, prominent in David's administration.
LEVITE, n. A member of the tribe of Levi, set apart for the service of the tabernacle and temple.
KOHATHITES, n. One of the three great Levitical divisions, descended from Kohath, charged with the sanctuary's holiest furniture.
OFFICER, n. One who holds a post of authority or trust in the administration of civil or ecclesiastical affairs.
VALOUR, n. Strength of mind in regard to danger; personal bravery; boldness in facing danger.
scriptures: Numbers 3:27
And of Kohath was the family of the Amramites, and the family of the Izeharites, and the family of the Hebronites, and the family of the Uzzielites: these are the families of the Kohathites.
Numbers 26:58

These are the families of the Levites: the family of the Libnites, the family of the Hebronites, the family of the Mahlites, the family of the Mushites, the family of the Korathites. And Kohath begat Amram.
1 Chronicles 26:30

And of the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his brethren, men of valour, a thousand and seven hundred, were officers among them of Israel on this side Jordan westward in all the business of the LORD, and in the service of the king.
1 Chronicles 23:19
Of the sons of Hebron; Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.
corruption_summary: The consistent, unglamorous census-list use of this clan name across Numbers and Chronicles, centuries apart, is the pattern of careful genealogical record-keeping, not late literary schematizing.
corruption_paragraphs: Source-critical theories that assign the priestly census material in Numbers to a late, artificial, post-exilic construction still have to account for the Chronicler's independent and internally consistent use of the same clan structure centuries afterward, right down to naming a fourth-generation officer roster. A late inventor working from imagination, not archive, does not typically reproduce a rival book's minor administrative clan names this precisely.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD's service under David extended past the altar into the ordinary work of the kingdom — men set apart from birth for sacred duty were also entrusted with civil administration, a pattern that refuses any hard sacred-secular divide and insists that all of life, rightly ordered under the LORD's law, is service to Him (Colossians 3:23–24).
roots_summary: Hebrew Chevroni (H2276), from Chevron (H2275); Qehathi (H6956), Kohathite; chayil (H2428), valour, strength; abodah (H5656), service, work.
roots_lines: Hebrew Chevroni (H2276) — Hebronite, from the ancestor Hebron son of Kohath.
Hebrew Qehathi (H6956) — Kohathite; the larger Levitical division the Hebronites belong to.
Hebrew chayil (H2428) — valour, strength, ability; the Chronicler's description of Hashabiah's men.
Hebrew abodah (H5656) — service, work; the word covering both sanctuary duty and the king's business.
Hebrew paqid (H6496), related to peqidah (H6486) — officer, overseer; the office David gave this clan.
usage: “The family of the Hebronites, and the family of the Uzzielites” — their place among the Kohathite clans.
“Men of valour... officers... in all the business of the LORD, and in the service of the king” — their role under David.
“Of the sons of Hebron; Jeriah the first” — the clan's own internal genealogy.

pos: n. (the clan descended from Zerah, son of Judah, that produced Achan's judgment and two of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Zarchi (H2227), from Zerach (Zerah), a son of Judah and Tamar; the -ite suffix marking clan membership.
biblical_def: The Zarhites take their name from Zerah, one of the twin sons Tamar bore to Judah (Genesis 38:30), and their clan appears twice in Scripture at moments of sharp contrast — disgrace and distinguished valor. The census of Judah names them among the tribe’s major divisions: “of Zerah, the family of the Zarhites” (Numbers 26:20). Their most infamous hour comes at Ai, where Joshua, seeking the sinner whose theft of the devoted things had brought defeat on Israel, narrows the search “family by family” — “he brought the family of Judah; and he took the family of the Zarhites: and he brought the family of the Zarhites man by man; and Zabdi was taken” (Joshua 7:17), the process that exposed Achan, Zabdi’s own grandson, as the man whose sin had brought a curse on the whole camp. Centuries later, under David, two of the kingdom’s most formidable mighty men come from this same disgraced clan, redeeming its name in valorous service: “Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zarhites” commanded twenty-four thousand men as the eighth monthly captain (1 Chronicles 27:11), and “Maharai the Netophathite, of the Zarhites” commanded an equal division as the tenth (1 Chronicles 27:13) — a single family line running from the shame of Achan’s theft at Ai to two captains of thousands guarding David’s throne.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Zarhites; they are the clan of Zerah son of Judah, the family from which the sinner Achan was exposed at Ai and, generations later, two of David's mighty captains descended.
webster_full: ZARHITES, n. A family of the tribe of Judah, descended from Zerah, prominent both in Achan's exposure and in David's mighty men.
ZERAH, n. A son of Judah by Tamar, twin brother of Pharez, ancestor of the Zarhite clan.
ACHAN, n. An Israelite of the tribe of Judah, of the Zarhite family, whose theft of devoted things brought judgment on Israel at Ai.
MIGHTY MEN, n. In Scripture, the title given to David's elite warriors, renowned for individual feats of valor and loyalty.
DEVOTED THING, n. In the Mosaic law, an object placed under a ban, wholly given over to the LORD and forbidden to private use.
scriptures: Numbers 26:20
And the sons of Judah after their families were; of Shelah, the family of the Shelanites: of Pharez, the family of the Pharzites: of Zerah, the family of the Zarhites.
Joshua 7:17
And he brought the family of Judah; and he took the family of the Zarhites: and he brought the family of the Zarhites man by man; and Zabdi was taken:
1 Chronicles 27:11
The eighth captain for the eighth month was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zarhites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand.
1 Chronicles 27:13
The tenth captain for the tenth month was Maharai the Netophathite, of the Zarhites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand.
corruption_summary: A single clan name tracked with narrative consistency from Genesis through Joshua into the David narratives, disgraced in one generation and honored in another, is exactly the kind of coherent, multi-book family memory a piecemeal legendary tradition rarely sustains.
corruption_paragraphs: Fragmentary source theories that treat Joshua's conquest narrative and Chronicles' court records as unrelated literary strata, compiled by different hands with no access to each other, are hard pressed to explain the seamless clan continuity here — the same Zarhite family name, correctly nested within Judah, correctly tied to Zerah, appears with total consistency across three separate books spanning Israel's history from Moses to David.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that neither individual sin nor family shame is the final word over a covenant line: Achan's theft brought death on himself and grief on Israel (Joshua 7:24–26), yet the very same clan, generations later, produced men whose valor is recorded among David's finest — a family's history under the LORD's covenant is never simply determined by its worst hour, and grace can raise up faithfulness from the same root that once bore judgment.
roots_summary: Hebrew Zarchi (H2227), from Zerach (H2226), Zerah, rising light; cherem (H2764), devoted thing, ban; gibbor (H1368), mighty man.
roots_lines: Hebrew Zarchi (H2227) — Zarhite, from the ancestor Zerah.
Hebrew Zerach (H2226) — Zerah, meaning rising or shining, the twin brother of Pharez.
Hebrew cherem (H2764) — devoted thing, the ban; the very thing Achan of this clan stole.
Hebrew gibbor (H1368) — mighty man; the title given to Sibbecai and Maharai, generations later.
Hebrew lakad (H3920) — to take, capture, seize by lot; the verb of Joshua's search that exposed Zabdi's house.
usage: “Of Zerah, the family of the Zarhites” — their place in the census of Judah.
“He took the family of the Zarhites... and Zabdi was taken” — the search that exposed Achan.
“Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zarhites” — the clan's later honor among David's captains.

pos: n. (the ancient kingdom of the Medes, allied with and eventually absorbed into Persia)
etymology: Hebrew Maday (H4074), Media, the Medes; a region of the Iranian plateau, conquered by and later dominant within the Persian empire.
biblical_def: Media is named repeatedly alongside Persia as one of the two allied kingdoms whose combined empire ruled the ancient world from Cyrus’s conquest of Babylon through the era of Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther. Ahasuerus’s court is described in terms of both nations together: “the power of Persia and Media, the nobles and princes of the provinces, being before him” (Esther 1:3), and his seven chief counselors are named as “the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king’s face” (Esther 1:14) — a formal court order in which Media, though the historically senior partner, had by this point yielded first place to Persia. Isaiah’s earlier oracle against Babylon summons Media by name as the LORD’s chosen instrument of judgment: “Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease” (Isaiah 21:2), a prophecy fulfilled when the combined Medo-Persian forces under Cyrus took Babylon. Daniel’s vision of the two-horned ram makes the historical relationship explicit: “the ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia” (Daniel 8:20), the lower horn (Media) rising first and the higher horn (Persia) rising after and outgrowing it — a detail matching the actual historical sequence in which Median power gave way to Persian dominance under Cyrus, even as the two nations continued to be named jointly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Media as an ancient country of Asia, whose people, the Medes, were united with the Persians under Cyrus; Scripture names Media alongside Persia throughout Esther, Isaiah, and Daniel.
webster_full: MEDIA, n. An ancient country of Asia, north of Persia, whose people were united with the Persians into a single empire under Cyrus.
MEDE, n. A native or inhabitant of Media.
PERSIA, n. An ancient empire of southwestern Asia, allied with and eventually dominant over Media.
PROPHECY, n. A declaration of something to come, made under divine inspiration; Isaiah's naming of Media generations before its rise.
EMPIRE, n. A large territory, or aggregate of states, under the government and dominion of a single ruler or sovereign power.
scriptures: Esther 1:3
In the third year of his reign, he made a feast unto all his princes and his servants; the power of Persia and Media, the nobles and princes of the provinces, being before him:
Esther 1:14
And the next unto him was Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom;
Isaiah 21:2
A grievous vision is declared unto me; the treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously, and the spoiler spoileth. Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease.
Daniel 8:20
The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia.
corruption_summary: A prophet naming Media, generations before its historical alliance with Persia became decisive, and getting the eventual order of dominance exactly right, is not the pattern of a prophecy written after the fact to fit known history.
corruption_paragraphs: Late-dating critical scholarship, eager to place Isaiah 21 and Daniel 8 after the events they describe precisely because their predictive accuracy seems otherwise inexplicable, has to reckon with the specific, falsifiable structure of the claims — Isaiah names Media as the LORD's chosen instrument against Babylon while Assyria, not the still-minor Babylon, was the reigning superpower of his own day, and Daniel's vision correctly predicts the order in which Media's earlier prominence would yield to Persia's later dominance rather than the reverse.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Daniel's own confession upon receiving these very visions of Gentile empires rising and falling in sequence: the LORD “changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Daniel 2:21). Media's rise, its yielding of precedence to Persia, and the whole empire's eventual fall to Greece were not accidents of geopolitics but stages the LORD had named and ordered toward the coming of an everlasting kingdom that no empire, however great, would supplant (Daniel 2:44).
roots_summary: Hebrew Maday (H4074), Media, the Medes; Paras (H6539), Persia; sar (H8269), prince, chief; malkuth (H4438), kingdom, royal power.
roots_lines: Hebrew Maday (H4074) — Media, the Medes; the older of the two allied powers.
Hebrew Paras (H6539) — Persia, Media's ally and eventual dominant partner.
Hebrew sar (H8269) — prince, chief; the officials named in Esther 1:14.
Hebrew malkuth (H4438) — kingdom, royal power; the word underlying Daniel's vision of shifting empires.
Hebrew chazon (H2377) — vision; the mode by which Isaiah and Daniel both received their word about Media.
usage: “The power of Persia and Media” — the joint empire at the height of its court ceremony.
“Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media” — Isaiah's prophecy of judgment on Babylon.
“The kings of Media and Persia” — Daniel's vision of the two-horned ram.
